html:
In October 1961 Turkey and West Germany signed a deal to recruit Turkish workers. It started one of the largest labour migrations of postwar Europe and built a Turkish community of millions in Germany.

West Germany's "economic miracle" needed workers, and the Berlin Wall, built that August, cut off the flow from East Germany. Similar deals already existed with Italy, Spain and Greece. Turkey had too many young men and too few jobs, and wanted their wages sent home.

The workers, called Gastarbeiter, "guest workers", were meant to stay a few years and rotate. They worked in mines, car plants and steel mills. Recruitment stopped in 1973, during the oil crisis, but many stayed and brought their families.

Today about three million people in Germany have Turkish roots, the largest such community outside Turkey. Germany was slow to accept them as citizens and only eased its citizenship law in 2000. Their story is part of a wider movement of workers toward richer countries, like Kerala workers to the Gulf and later Syrian refugees.
sum: In October 1961 Turkey and West Germany signed a deal to recruit Turkish workers. It started one of the largest labour migrations of postwar Europe and built a Turkish community of millions in Germany.
